# Browser sequence comparison — 2026-11-09

Independent local captures: Chromium **156.0.8078.79**, Firefox **159.0.1**,
macOS, new headless profiles. Each of ten cases contains 11 browser requests,
11 Surf preset requests and 11 Surf requests with exactly the browser's input
fields: **330 requests total**. Each JSON preserves browser field order and raw
HPACK/QPACK blocks, browser metadata, pcap SHA-256, control streams, comparison
rows and independent decoding status. Browser blocks are never generated by Surf.

## Current HPACK regression

Chromium's **11/11 raw HPACK blocks now match these original browser bytes**,
including the 128-byte table, zero capacity, oversized entries, subsequent table
references, cookies, authorization and growth to 65536. The test compares whole
blocks for Chromium. Firefox's eleven exact field encodings and its table updates
also remain covered, with only the documented initial SETTINGS placement race
handled separately. Both sequences pass repeated replay with the race detector.

Chrome desktop and Android select first-static-name lookup and incremental
oversized insertion through Surf's profile builders. Android shares the codec
policy; this desktop capture does not independently establish Android parity.

The JSON files and their comparison rows below retain the **capture-time**
results from Surf v1.0.211. They have not been rewritten from Surf output.
HTTP/3 results and resource-context differences are outside this HPACK change.

## Capture-time results (Surf v1.0.211)

These historical rows describe v1.0.211. Current outgoing dynamic QPACK and
Huffman policies are verified separately in the [QPACK audit](../qpack/README.md).
The original browser fixtures below remain unchanged.

| Comparison using identical ordered input fields | Observed result |
| --- | --- |
| All ten cases | All 11 decoded request field sequences match, including Cookie and Authorization |
| Firefox HTTP/2, repeated/changing table settings | 11/11 raw HPACK blocks match byte for byte in this capture |
| Chromium HTTP/2 | 0/11 raw blocks match; decoded fields match in order and value |
| Firefox HTTP/3, peer capacity 0 | 11/11 raw QPACK blocks match byte for byte |
| Chromium HTTP/3, peer capacity 0 | Field representations and sizes match, but string Huffman bits/bytes differ |
| Both browsers, HTTP/3 peer capacity 128/4096/65536 | Browsers use dynamic QPACK; Surf sends static field sections |
| HTTP/3 SETTINGS | Ordered IDs/values match after excluding random GREASE settings |
| HTTP/3 initial PRIORITY_UPDATE | Chromium sends one for each request; Firefox sends none in this scenario; Surf matches when supplied the same Priority inputs |
| HTTP/3 Cookie fields | Chromium splits pairs; Firefox sends one combined field; Surf matches both |

The Firefox HTTP/2 first two blocks can differ between separate runs only in
where the initial 4096-byte size update occurs: initial SETTINGS can arrive
before or after the first request. The offline test therefore checks the
aggregate update sequence separately from each exact field encoding. Later
shrink/grow/repeated updates, eviction, changed credentials and cookie boundaries
remain covered on one connection. This capture includes growth to **65536**;
the old Go encoder limit of 4096 is absent.

Chromium HPACK uses name index **4** for literal `:path`; Surf's original default
static lookup used **5**. With a 128-byte table, Chromium emits incremental literals
even for oversized regular fields, which clear its table; Surf originally used
the Go encoder's without-indexing literals instead. That changed later table
references. With capacity zero, the representation difference persisted. At
capture time, for `/step/4`,
`/step/5`, `/step/6`, browser/Surf blocks are respectively **593/595**,
**582/563**, **575/584** bytes. The current Chromium replay matches **593**,
**582**, **575** bytes exactly, including all field bytes and table updates.

Chromium QPACK Huffman-encodes strings only when it reduces their size. The
official encoder used by Surf also encodes equal-size strings. For example,
`sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0` and `sec-ch-ua-platform: "macOS"` differ in Huffman bits
at capacity zero even though field section lengths are equal. Firefox's static
blocks match Surf, including this scenario's credentials. Its HTTP/3 behavior
must not be inferred from its different HPACK sensitivity rules.

At peer capacity 4096, Chromium's warmed `/step/2` block is **24** bytes versus
Surf's **583**. Firefox's is **414** versus **483**. These are field section
sizes only: browsers also send encoder-stream instructions (stored in each
fixture), so the numbers are not total network cost or a compression benchmark.
Firefox reuses dynamic names/references; Chromium also indexes repeated values.
At capacity 65536 the chosen encoder capacity is 65536 in both browser captures
(capacity instruction `3fe1ff03`). The earlier report's value 4096 was a prefixed-
integer interpretation error; the saved raw captures were correct.
The first request can be static if it precedes the peer SETTINGS.

QPACK stream assignments agree where transmitted: Chromium control stream 2,
encoder 10; Firefox control 2, encoder 6, decoder 10. Chromium's decoder 6
does not transmit in this static-response scenario. At capacity zero Chromium
still transmits stream 10's type plus `Set Dynamic Table Capacity(0)`; Surf
currently leaves its lazy encoder stream silent. Firefox eagerly transmits
both QPACK stream types in both implementations. Observed arrival order across
independent streams is not a reservation-order or scheduling guarantee.

GREASE control frames were observed for both browsers and Surf. Their random
IDs/payloads are retained for inspection, not compared for literal equality.
No request-stream GREASE frame appeared in these 11-request browser sequences;
that does not establish that browsers never send them. Reprioritization of an
already open request was not triggered by this scenario.

## Preset headers versus browser resource context

Surf's navigation preset is not an automatic implementation of JavaScript fetch.
Real fetches changed field order and values: `Referer`, `Pragma`, `Cache-Control`,
`Accept`, `Sec-Fetch-*` and `Priority`; `Upgrade-Insecure-Requests` and
`Sec-Fetch-User` disappeared. Chromium's fetch priority was `u=1, i`, while a
plain Surf preset GET remained `u=0, i`. Feeding the same captured Priority into
Surf produced the same eleven PRIORITY_UPDATE stream IDs/values as Chromium.

The installed Chromium is an unbranded headless build: its UA contains
`HeadlessChrome` and its client hints omit the Google Chrome brand. Surf's branded
Chrome navigation profile is not changed to match those automation-specific
values. Browser language and OS choices also remain explicit input differences.

## Independent verification and limits

Wireshark 4.6.9 independently decoded **317/330** request field sections. Its
decoded names, values and order match the receiving peer in all 317. It emitted
no decoded fields for 13 dynamic browser sections (Chromium capacity 128: 8;
Firefox capacity 128: 1; Firefox capacity 4096 and 65536: 2 each). These sections
retain raw bytes and peer-decoded fields and are marked
`independent_fields_decoded: false`. They are not counted as independent decoder
matches. Surf's 220 sections were all independently decoded. A separate bounded
RFC 9204 syntax parser verified representation counts and N/Huffman bits for
all 264 HTTP/3 sections. HTTP/2 raw blocks were also checked against the peer.

This experiment captures exact TLS streams/UDP datagrams with **synthetic
IP/TCP envelopes**, not a privileged NIC capture. It cannot validate packet
pacing, TCP segmentation, congestion, loss recovery, scheduling or IP/TCP
fingerprints. Its private files contain only synthetic local traffic. TLS keys,
browser profiles and certificates are not committed. This is not a new audit
of TLS ClientHello fingerprints; the existing independent TLS/Initial tests
continue to cover those. Mobile browsers and different resource workloads
require their own captures.

Reproduction and fixture refresh: [capture tool](../../../tools/wirecapture/README.md).
Offline tests: `TestIndependentBrowserHTTP2Sequence` in the capture tool package
checks Chromium's complete raw blocks, Firefox's exact field encodings, both
browsers' field order/values and table update sequences.
`TestIndependentBrowserHTTP3Sequence` checks both
browsers' exact ordered fields and SETTINGS, Chromium priorities and all eleven
exact zero-capacity QPACK blocks for each browser. Fresh dynamic-table comparisons
are recorded in the [QPACK audit](../qpack/README.md).

## Browser source references

Chromium 156.0.8078.79 pins Quiche revision
`a1628192cf32ba40d21e0dd80f485d68c24ff87a` in its
[DEPS](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/156.0.8078.79/DEPS).
The [HPACK encoder](https://github.com/google/quiche/blob/a1628192cf32ba40d21e0dd80f485d68c24ff87a/quiche/http2/hpack/hpack_encoder.cc)
and [QPACK string encoding](https://github.com/google/quiche/blob/a1628192cf32ba40d21e0dd80f485d68c24ff87a/quiche/quic/core/qpack/qpack_instruction_encoder.cc)
explain the observed literal and Huffman choices. Firefox references are pinned
to `FIREFOX_159_0_1_RELEASE`:
[HPACK](https://github.com/mozilla-firefox/firefox/blob/FIREFOX_159_0_1_RELEASE/netwerk/protocol/http/Http2Compression.cpp),
[vendored QPACK](https://github.com/mozilla-firefox/firefox/blob/FIREFOX_159_0_1_RELEASE/third_party/rust/neqo-qpack/src/encoder.rs),
[HTTP/3 setup](https://github.com/mozilla-firefox/firefox/blob/FIREFOX_159_0_1_RELEASE/third_party/rust/neqo-http3/src/connection.rs),
and [local Alt-Svc mapping](https://github.com/mozilla-firefox/firefox/blob/FIREFOX_159_0_1_RELEASE/netwerk/protocol/http/nsHttpHandler.cpp).
